title: Food Truck Best Stretch
aka: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
story: You run a food truck and keep a log of each day's profit. Rainy days, broken fryers and festival fees mean some days lose money, so the log has negative numbers too.
A magazine wants to feature your truck and asks for your best run of exactly k days in a row. You want to know the highest total profit any k consecutive days in your log reached.
task: Write bestStretch(profits, k). Return the largest sum of any k consecutive entries of profits.
The answer can be negative if every stretch of k days lost money.

examples.explanation: The 3-day stretches add up to 120 - 40 + 300 = 380, then -40 + 300 + 80 = 340, then 300 + 80 - 200 = 180, then 80 - 200 + 150 = 30. The best is 380, from the first three days.
Every 2-day stretch lost money: -70, -110, -100. The best is -70. If you start your running best at 0, you would wrongly answer 0.

hints: In the first example, the stretch of days 0 to 2 sums to 380. The next stretch is days 1 to 3. Which days do the two stretches share?
Two neighbouring stretches share all but one day at each end. Moving one day to the right drops the oldest day and adds one new day.
So you never need to add up k numbers again. You can update the previous total with one subtraction and one addition.
Sum the first k days and make that your best so far. Then for each next day i, add profits[i], subtract profits[i - k], and keep the largest total you see.
bruteForce: For every starting day, add up the next k profits, and keep the largest total.

That is about n × k additions. With 10,000 days and k = 5,000 it is roughly 25 million additions, almost all of them repeated: neighbouring stretches share k - 1 days, and you add those same days up again every time.

total += profits[i] - profits[i - k]; // add the new day, drop the oldest

walkthrough: Think of a frame exactly k days wide lying on the log. Sliding it one day to the right lets one day in on the right and pushes one day out on the left. Everything in between stays, so the total changes by just those two days.
• Slide: add day 3 (80), drop day 0 (120). 380 + 80 - 120 = 340. Best stays 380.
• Slide: add day 4 (-200), drop day 1 (-40). 340 - 200 + 40 = 180. Best stays 380.
• Slide: add day 5 (150), drop day 2 (300). 180 + 150 - 300 = 30. Best stays 380.
Each slide costs two operations, whatever k is. Start best at the first frame's total, not at 0, so an all-losing log still gives the right answer.
solution.timeWhy: k additions for the first frame, then two operations per slide.
solution.spaceWhy: Just the running total and the best total.
solution.takeaway: For a fixed-size window, keep a running total and update it as the window slides: add what enters, subtract what leaves. The same idea works for running counts, averages and character tallies.
